prompt:
Suppose that a group $G$ is the (internal) direct product of subgroups $S$ and $T$. Let $H$ be a subgroup of $G$ such that $SH=G=TH$.

(a) Prove that $S\cap H$ and $T\cap H$ are normal subgroups of $G$.

(b) If $S\cap H=1=T\cap H$, prove that $S$ and $T$ are isomorphic.

(c) If $S\cap H=1=T\cap H$ and $H$ is normal in $G$, show that $G$ is abelian.
answer: (a) $S\cap H\trianglelefteq H$, and $T$ centralizes $S$, so $N_G(S\cap H)\supseteq HT=G$. (b) $T\cong G/S=SH/S\cong H$ and likewise $S\cong H$. (c) $[H,S]\subseteq H\cap S=1$ and $[H,T]=1$, so $C_G(S)\supseteq HT=G$ and $C_G(T)\supseteq HS=G$; thus $G=ST$ is central.

solutions.title: Commuting direct factors
solutions.body:
Since $S,T\trianglelefteq G$ and $S\cap T=1$, $[S,T]\subseteq S\cap T=1$, so $S$ and $T$ commute elementwise.

**(a)** As $S\trianglelefteq G$, $S\cap H\trianglelefteq H$. Also $T$ centralizes $S\cap H\subseteq S$, so $T$ normalizes it. Hence $N_G(S\cap H)\supseteq HT=G$, i.e. $S\cap H\trianglelefteq G$. The argument for $T\cap H$ is symmetric (using $G=SH$).

**(b)** By the second isomorphism theorem, $G/S=SH/S\cong H/(S\cap H)\cong H$. Since $G=S\times T$, $G/S\cong T$. So $T\cong H$, and by symmetry $S\cong H$; hence $S\cong T$.

**(c)** With $H\trianglelefteq G$: $[H,S]\subseteq H\cap S=1$ and $[H,T]\subseteq H\cap T=1$. So $H$ centralizes $S$ and $T$. Then $C_G(S)\supseteq HT=G$ and $C_G(T)\supseteq HS=G$, so $S,T\subseteq Z(G)$ and $G=ST\subseteq Z(G)$: $G$ is abelian. ∎

prompt:
Let $A_1,A_2,\ldots,A_n$ be ideals of the commutative ring $R$, and let $D=\bigcap_{i=1}^nA_i$.

(a) Prove that $\sqrt{D}=\bigcap_{i=1}^n\sqrt{A_i}$.

(b) Now suppose that $D$ is a primary ideal and that it is not the intersection of any proper subset of $\{A_1,A_2,\ldots,A_n\}$. Show that $\sqrt{A_i}=\sqrt{D}$ for all $i$.
answer: (a) If $r^{m_i}\in A_i$ then $r^{\max m_i}\in D$. (b) For $r^m\in A_i$ pick $s\in\bigcap_{j\neq i}A_j\setminus D$; then $r^ms\in D$ with $s\notin D$, so $(r^m)^t\in D$ and $r\in\sqrt D$.

prompt:
Let $K\subseteq E$ be a finite degree extension of fields of characteristic $0$, and let $F_1$ and $F_2$ be intermediate fields. These intermediate fields are said to be linearly disjoint over $K$ if $|\langle F_1,F_2\rangle:K|=|F_1:K|\,|F_2:K|$, where $\langle F_1,F_2\rangle$ is the subfield of $E$ generated by $F_1$ and $F_2$.

(a) Prove that $|\langle F_1,F_2\rangle:F_1|\le|F_2:K|$ for any $F_1$ and $F_2$.

(b) If $|F_1:K|$ and $|F_2:K|$ are relatively prime, prove that $F_1$ and $F_2$ are linearly disjoint over $K$.

(c) Give an example with $|F_1:K|=2=|F_2:K|$ to show that fields can be linearly disjoint without having relatively prime degrees.

(d) If $F_1$ and $F_2$ are linearly disjoint and Galois over $K$, prove that the Galois groups satisfy $\mathrm{Gal}(\langle F_1,F_2\rangle/K)\cong\mathrm{Gal}(F_1/K)\times\mathrm{Gal}(F_2/K)$.
answer: (a) For a $K$-basis $a_1,\dots,a_n$ of $F_2$, $\sum F_1a_k$ is a ring, finite-dimensional over $F_1$ and a domain, hence a field, so it is $\langle F_1,F_2\rangle$. (b) Both degrees divide $|\langle F_1,F_2\rangle:K|\le|F_1:K||F_2:K|$. (c) $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2)$, $\mathbb{Q}(i)$. (d) Restriction gives an injection into the product, and orders agree.

solutions.title: Spanning sets and degree counting
solutions.body:
Let $F=\langle F_1,F_2\rangle$.

**(a)** Let $a_1,\dots,a_n$ be a $K$-basis of $F_2$, $n=|F_2:K|$, and $L=\sum_kF_1a_k$. Each $a_ia_j\in F_2=\sum_kKa_k$, so $L$ is closed under multiplication; it is a subring of $E$ containing $F_1$ and $F_2$, an integral domain, and a finite-dimensional $F_1$-vector space. A finite-dimensional domain over a field is a field (multiplication by a nonzero element is injective, hence surjective). So $L$ is a field containing $F_1,F_2$, contained in $F$; thus $L=F$, and $|F:F_1|\le n$ since $a_1,\dots,a_n$ span.

**(b)** By (a), $|F:K|=|F:F_1|\,|F_1:K|\le|F_2:K|\,|F_1:K|$. Both $|F_1:K|$ and $|F_2:K|$ divide $|F:K|$, and they are coprime, so their product divides $|F:K|$. Hence equality.

**(c)** $K=\mathbb{Q}$, $F_1=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2)$, $F_2=\mathbb{Q}(i)$ inside $E=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2,i)$. Since $F_1\subset\mathbb{R}$, $i\notin F_1$, so $|F:F_1|=|F_1(i):F_1|=2$ and $|F:\mathbb{Q}|=4=2\cdot2$.

**(d)** $F/K$ is Galois (compositum of Galois extensions: splitting field of the product of the defining polynomials). Restriction gives a homomorphism $\theta\colon\mathrm{Gal}(F/K)\to\mathrm{Gal}(F_1/K)\times\mathrm{Gal}(F_2/K)$; if $\sigma\in\ker\theta$, it fixes $F_1$ and $F_2$, hence $F$, so $\theta$ is injective. Orders: $|\mathrm{Gal}(F/K)|=|F:K|=|F_1:K||F_2:K|$, which is the order of the product. So $\theta$ is an isomorphism. ∎

prompt:
Let $V$ be a complex vector space, not necessarily of finite dimension. Suppose that $A,B\colon V\to V$ are nonzero $\mathbb{C}$-linear transformations with $AB=\lambda BA$ for some fixed nonzero complex number $\lambda$. Assume that no proper subspace of $V$ is invariant under both $A$ and $B$. That is, if $W$ is a subspace of $V$ with $AW\subseteq W$ and $BW\subseteq W$, then $W=0$ or $V$.

(a) Show that $A$ and $B$ are both one-to-one and onto.

(b) If $V$ is finite dimensional, prove that $\lambda$ is a root of unity.

(c) Show that a finite-dimensional example exists with $\lambda=-1$.
answer: (a) $\ker A$ and $\operatorname{im}A$ (and likewise for $B$) are invariant under both, so are $0$ resp. $V$. (b) $\det A\det B=\lambda^n\det B\det A$ with nonzero determinants gives $\lambda^n=1$. (c) $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$, $B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ on $\mathbb{C}^2$.

solutions.title: Invariant kernels and images
solutions.body:
**(a)** Let $N=\ker A$. Clearly $AN=0\subseteq N$; and for $v\in N$, $A(Bv)=\lambda B(Av)=0$, so $BN\subseteq N$. Hence $N=0$ or $V$; $N=V$ means $A=0$, excluded. So $A$ is injective. Let $I=AV$. Then $AI\subseteq I$ and $B(Av)=\lambda^{-1}A(Bv)\in I$. So $I=0$ or $V$; $I=0$ means $A=0$. So $A$ is onto. Using $BA=\lambda^{-1}AB$, the same arguments show $\ker B$ and $BV$ are invariant under both, so $B$ is one-to-one and onto.

**(b)** Let $n=\dim V$ (finite, and $n\ge1$ since $A\ne0$). Taking determinants in $AB=\lambda BA$ gives $\det A\det B=\lambda^n\det B\det A$. By (a), $\det A,\det B\neq0$, so $\lambda^n=1$.

**(c)** On $V=\mathbb{C}^2$ let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$, $B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Then $AB=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}=-BA$. A proper nonzero invariant subspace would be a line invariant under $A$, hence $\mathbb{C}e_1$ or $\mathbb{C}e_2$ (the eigenspaces of $A$, as its eigenvalues are distinct); but $B$ swaps $e_1$ and $e_2$. So no proper nonzero subspace is invariant under both. ∎

prompt:
Let $R$ be a ring and let $Z$ denote its center. A derivation $D\colon R\to R$ is a map satisfying $D(a+b)=D(a)+D(b)$ and $D(ab)=aD(b)+D(a)b$ for all $a,b\in R$.

(a) If $r\in R$, show that the map $A_r\colon R\to R$ given by $A_r(a)=ar-ra$, for all $a\in R$, is a derivation of $R$.

(b) If $D$ is a derivation of $R$, prove that $D(Z)\subseteq Z$.

(c) If $D$ is a derivation of $R$ and $e\in Z$ is an idempotent, prove that $D(e)=0$. (Hint. You may need to evaluate $(1-2e)^2$.)
answer: (a) Direct computation: $abr-rab=a(br-rb)+(ar-ra)b$. (b) Apply $D$ to $rz=zr$ and use $zD(r)=D(r)z$. (c) $D(e)=D(e^2)=2eD(e)$, so $(1-2e)D(e)=0$; multiply by $1-2e$, using $(1-2e)^2=1$.

solutions.title: Direct computation
solutions.body:
**(a)** $A_r(a+b)=(a+b)r-r(a+b)=A_r(a)+A_r(b)$, and
$$A_r(ab)=abr-rab=a(br-rb)+(ar-ra)b=aA_r(b)+A_r(a)b.$$

**(b)** Let $z\in Z$, $r\in R$. Applying $D$ to $rz=zr$:
$$rD(z)+D(r)z=D(rz)=D(zr)=zD(r)+D(z)r.$$
Since $z$ is central, $D(r)z=zD(r)$, leaving $rD(z)=D(z)r$. So $D(z)\in Z$.

**(c)** (Here $R$ has $1$, as in the hint.) By (b), $D(e)\in Z$, so $e$ and $D(e)$ commute, and
$$D(e)=D(e^2)=eD(e)+D(e)e=2eD(e).$$
Thus $(1-2e)D(e)=0$. Now $(1-2e)^2=1-4e+4e^2=1$, so multiplying on the left by $1-2e$ gives $D(e)=0$. ∎
